item.title: Sushila G. — Friendly Hindi Tutor — Speak, Read & Write with Confidence
item.description: Hello! My name is Sashi, and I am a passionate Hindi tutor. I love teaching Hindi and helping students learn in an easy, fun and effective way. I have experience working with learners of every level, whether you are a complete beginner or looking to improve your fluency. Lessons $6 per 50 min.

item.title: Hemlata — Native Hindi Tutor for Kids, Adults & Beginners — Read, Write & Speak
item.description: Namaste! I am Hemlata, a native Hindi speaker and tutor. I teach kids, adults and complete beginners, and I adapt every lesson to the age and level of the student in front of me. Lessons $12 per 50 min.

item.title: Shikha Dutta — Experienced Hindi Tutor for Classes 1–10 — Devanagari, Grammar & Confident Speaking
item.description: I am Shikha Dutta, and I have sixteen years of teaching experience, seven of those teaching online. I teach students from Class 1 through to Class 10, and I currently have thirty-two students in India and abroad learning Hindi with me. Lessons $8 per 50 min.

item.title: Tara — Native Hindi Tutor — Conversation, Grammar & Script for Every Level
item.description: Namaste! I am Tara, a native Hindi speaker and tutor. I enjoy helping students find their confidence in Hindi, whether they are starting from zero or polishing skills they already have. Lessons $8 per 50 min.

item.title: The Hindi Alphabet: A Complete Beginner's Guide to Devanagari
item.description: Learn every Hindi letter with its sound and an English example. Vowels, consonants and matras explained simply, with a printable chart and the order to learn them in.

item.title: How to Say Hello in Hindi — And When Namaste Is the Wrong Word
item.description: Namaste is not the only Hindi greeting, and sometimes it is the wrong one. A practical guide to greeting people in Hindi by time, age, religion and situation.

item.title: Hindi Numbers 1 to 100 — Why They Are Hard, and How to Learn Them Anyway
item.description: Hindi numbers are genuinely irregular, unlike most languages. Here is the full 1–100 list with pronunciation, plus the pattern that makes them learnable and the shortcut Indians actually use.

item.title: How to Actually Learn Hindi Online in 2026 — An Honest Guide
item.description: Apps, YouTube, textbooks or a tutor? A frank comparison of every way to learn Hindi online, what each one is genuinely good for, and roughly how long fluency takes.

item.title: 50 Hindi Phrases for Travelling in India — What You Will Actually Use
item.description: The Hindi phrases that genuinely matter when travelling in India: bargaining, autos, trains, food and being unwell. Written by people who use them, not copied from a phrasebook.

item.title: How to Write Your Name in Hindi — With the Full Letter Guide
item.description: Write any English name in Devanagari, letter by letter. A complete sound-to-letter table, worked examples for common names, and the four mistakes everyone makes.

item.title: Hindi Family Words — Why There Are Twelve Words for Cousin
item.description: Every Hindi family relation with pronunciation, and the logic behind why Hindi has separate words for your father's brother and your mother's brother when English does not.

item.title: Hindi vs Urdu — What Is Actually Different, and What Is Not
item.description: Hindi and Urdu speakers understand each other completely, yet the languages are treated as separate. A clear explanation of the script, vocabulary and history behind the split.

item.title: Days, Months and Telling the Time in Hindi
item.description: The days of the week, the months, and how to tell the time in Hindi — including dhai and saadhe, the half-hour words that confuse every learner.

item.title: Learning Hindi from Bollywood — Which Films, and What It Will Not Teach You
item.description: Films are a genuinely good way to learn Hindi, if you pick the right ones and use them properly. Recommendations by level, plus an honest list of what film Hindi gets wrong.

item.title: Hindi Gender — Why Your Verb Changes Depending on Who Is Speaking
item.description: Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine, and the verb changes with the speaker's own gender. The rules, the patterns that let you guess, and the exceptions worth memorising.

item.title: Hindi Word Order — Why the Verb Goes Last
item.description: Hindi puts the verb at the end and postpositions after the noun. Once you see the pattern, sentences stop feeling backwards. With worked examples and the questions that trip people up.

item.title: Aap, Tum or Tu — Getting Politeness Right in Hindi
item.description: Hindi has three words for you, and choosing wrong can be genuinely rude. Who gets which, how the verb changes with each, and the safe default when you are unsure.

item.title: 10 Mistakes Every Hindi Learner Makes — And How to Stop
item.description: The errors that mark you out as a learner, why each one happens, and the fix. Written from what actually goes wrong in lessons, not from a textbook.

item.title: Hindi Verbs — Present, Past and Future in One Page
item.description: Every Hindi tense you need to hold a conversation, with the endings laid out plainly. Includes the ne rule that catches everyone and the honest shortcut for beginners.

item.title: How do you apologise in Hindi?
item.description: माफ़ कीजिए (maaf keejiye) for a real apology, सॉरी — the English word — for a small everyday one. Hindi speakers use the English 'sorry' constantly and nobody considers it lazy.

item.title: What is the hardest part of learning Hindi?
item.description: For most learners it is grammatical gender — every noun is masculine or feminine, there is no reliable rule, and the verb agrees too. The pronunciation gets more attention but is a smaller problem.

item.title: Can I learn Hindi just by watching Bollywood?
item.description: You can build a very good ear and a large passive vocabulary. You cannot learn to speak, and you will pick up a register that sounds wrong in ordinary conversation.

item.title: How many Hindi words do I need to know?
item.description: About 500 words for everyday survival, 1,500 for comfortable conversation, and around 3,000 to follow a film without subtitles. The first 200 do most of the work.

item.title: Is Hindi harder than Spanish?
item.description: For an English speaker, yes — noticeably. Spanish shares an alphabet, much vocabulary and a similar sentence order. Hindi shares none of those, though its grammar is more regular than Spanish grammar once you are in.

item.title: How can I practise speaking Hindi if I have nobody to talk to?
item.description: Speak aloud anyway — narrate what you are doing, record sixty seconds and listen back. It is worth much less than a real conversation and much more than silent study.

item.title: Am I too old to learn Hindi?
item.description: No. Adults learn grammar and vocabulary faster than children; children win only on accent, and even that gap is smaller than people think. Time on task matters far more than age.

item.title: How do I remember whether a Hindi noun is masculine or feminine?
item.description: Learn the gender with the noun, never separately, and use the endings as a rough guide: most nouns ending in आ are masculine and most ending in ई are feminine — with real exceptions.

item.title: Will Hindi speakers mind if I make mistakes?
item.description: Almost universally no — the reaction to a foreigner attempting Hindi is warmth, not correction. The bigger risk is being answered in English out of helpfulness.

item.title: What does namaste actually mean?
item.description: Roughly "I bow to you" — नमः (a bow) plus ते (to you). In India it is an ordinary polite greeting, not the spiritual formula it has become in yoga studios abroad.

item.title: How long does it take to learn to read Devanagari?
item.description: Most learners read simple words within four to six weeks of regular practice, and read fluently — without sounding out — in about six months.

item.title: How do you say thank you in Hindi?
item.description: The two everyday words are शुक्रिया (shukriya) and धन्यवाद (dhanyavaad). In ordinary conversation most people say shukriya; dhanyavaad is more formal and can sound stiff between friends.

item.title: How do you say hello in Hindi?
item.description: नमस्ते (namaste) works at any time of day and is never wrong. Press your palms together at chest height and dip your head slightly. Among friends, क्या हाल है? (kya haal hai?) is more natural.

item.title: How do you say I love you in Hindi?
item.description: मैं तुमसे प्यार करता हूँ (main tumse pyaar karta hoon) if you are male, मैं तुमसे प्यार करती हूँ (main tumse pyaar karti hoon) if you are female. The verb ending changes with the speaker's gender, not the listener's.
